title: Sun and Steel: The Book That Changes Lives
summary: First episode of NH's analysis of Yukio Mishima's Sun and Steel: the 'boy without a body' corroded by words, the language of the body versus the language of the flesh, lifting as wordless ritual, the body as a canvas and garden, and an 'aristocracy of the body' earned daily through effort. He ties these themes to natural bodybuilding, rejection of mind-body dualism, PED users' 'abomination' physiques, and building identity through solitary training.
claims: Sun and Steel is not a Bushido commandment book like Musashi's; it is introspective 'confidential criticism' mixing nostalgic confession with analytical criticism of one's past
Mishima's vulnerability, presenting himself as the opposite of a hero, makes him more relatable than Musashi
Mishima was a bookish, weak child whose physicality was wasted by words; he discovered his 'backbone' too late
As a nerdy kid NH latched onto being 'smart' and looked down on athletic kids out of envy; people double down on flaws by calling them strengths
Words reduce reality to abstraction and corrode it; the body must be known through the body, not through language
Lifting is a purely physical activity that needs no words, which is why Mishima turned to bodybuilding
Over-intellectualised modern fitness produces 'boys without bodies' who approach lifting only through language
The ideal is the complete man, like the samurai: physically capable and intellectually educated; maxing one side only makes you incomplete
Being proud of not being physical doesn't make you smarter, it makes you incomplete
A brain without bodily experience digests itself, and a body without a brain is equally an abomination; mind and body must work together
The body is a canvas: lifters reject being a default character and become a custom character, the shipwright of their own body
Lifters are a minority who took control of their bodies; fake humility about being no better than average should be dropped and the effort taken pride in
Bodybuilding is the pursuit and protection of beauty, a transcendent value that cannot be described in words but is recognised on sight
You can't understand lifting until you do it; NH mocked lifters before he lifted
While lifting, NH sees nothing: no mirror, walls or people; lifting makes existence tolerable for a moment
Humans create sacred meaning and beauty; lifting is important because you decide it is
Lifting feeds the spark of divinity in you; that's not narcissism
The shared experience of training unites all lifters in brotherhood regardless of goals or background
An 'aristocracy of the body' is earned through the choice of physical exertion, not inherited, and is lost if you stop lifting
Lifters are fitter than 99% of the population because they chose to train, not because of genetics
If you have to ask to be seen as special, you're not special; status claimed through language without effort is hollow
When one person in a mediocre group becomes excellent, the others resent the comparison and try to drag him back
Modern men are over-domesticated with too little Dionysian chaotic energy; lifting is aggression and madness that produces Apollonian beauty
Like sex, lifting can only be understood by experiencing it; no amount of reading replaces doing
Mind and body grow together or perish together; Mishima was a pioneer of natural bodybuilding's holistic aim
NH would give up all his muscle to keep the spiritual gains from lifting
Lifters who stagnate often do so because their mind stopped growing, and these are the ones who turn to PEDs as a shortcut
PED users try to hack nature to look superhuman but end up looking non-human, an 'abomination'
You don't need superhuman willpower to start; advanced lifters weren't special, they decided to be, and body and willpower build each other
Natural limits are safeguards that maintain the body's harmony; the more advanced a natural gets, the less appealing PED physiques look
Advanced natural lifters are all quirky individuals; novices form an undifferentiated mass because they don't yet know what they want
Training forces isolation and patience that build identity; best done in your teens before responsibilities
Social media turned fitness into clone wars where young men copy influencers instead of building their own identity
You can choose not to garden, but you can't choose not to have a garden; neglect lets weeds take over
